title: How to give a home robot or smart device its own Wi-Fi network
excerpt: Putting robots, cameras and other smart devices on a separate home network limits what an attacker can reach if one of them is hacked. Here is how to do it, step by step.

sources.title: US National Security Agency: Best Practices for Securing Your Home Network (Cybersecurity Information Sheet, February 2023)
GOV.UK (Department for Science, Innovation and Technology): Smart devices: using them safely in your home

body_html:
Most homes run everything on one Wi-Fi network: laptops, phones, televisions, cameras, speakers and, more and more, robots. That is convenient, but it means that if one weak device is hacked, the attacker may be able to reach everything else on the same network.

A simple way to reduce that risk is to put smart devices on a network of their own. Security agencies recommend it. Guidance from the US National Security Agency says: "At a minimum, your wireless network should be segmented between your primary Wi-Fi, guest Wi-Fi, and IoT network." (IoT, the "Internet of Things", means everyday devices connected to the internet.) The point, it explains, is to stop less secure devices from talking directly to the devices you trust most.

What "its own network" means

You do not need a second internet connection. Most home routers can create more than one Wi-Fi network from the same box. The usual options are:

  • A guest network: a separate Wi-Fi name and password, often kept apart from your main network by default.
  • A dedicated smart-device network: some routers offer a network set aside for smart devices.
  • A separate segment (VLAN): a more advanced option on some routers and business equipment.

Your router's manual or the maker's support pages will say which of these it offers.

Step by step

  1. Update the router first. Install updates, ideally automatically. The NSA guidance also advises replacing a router once it no longer receives security support.
  2. Secure the router itself. Use a strong administrator password, turn off remote administration, and turn off Universal Plug and Play (UPnP), a feature that lets devices open connections through the router on their own.
  3. Create the second network. Give it its own name and a long passphrase. Use WPA3 encryption where your devices support it, or WPA2/WPA3 mixed mode for older ones.
  4. Move the smart devices. Connect robots, cameras, speakers, smart plugs and similar devices to the new network. Keep computers and phones with personal data on the main one.
  5. Check each device still works. Some devices are set up through a phone app. If one stops responding after the move, check the maker's instructions before changing anything else.

What it does not fix

A separate network limits the damage if a device is hacked. It does not make a weak device secure. The basics still apply. The UK government's smart-device guidance advises changing any easily guessed factory password, turning on two-step login (two-factor authentication) where it is offered, and switching on automatic updates. If you think someone has taken control of a device, it advises a factory reset, and it recommends a factory reset before you sell or give a device away.

The NSA guidance adds some habits for devices with sensors: mute microphones and cover cameras when they are not needed, disconnect devices you rarely use, and update them before using them again.

Why it matters for people staying in charge

A robot or camera in your home should answer to you, not to whoever manages to reach it. Keeping devices updated and supported is D6 Secure and supported. Keeping their sensors away from strangers is D5 Private by default. And making sure only you can tell a device what to do supports D1 Always stoppable. A hacked robot is one nobody is in charge of.

Network separation is something you can do yourself today. The rest, such as secure defaults and long security support, is up to makers. Our security page and questions to ask can help when you are choosing a device.
